html:
The Xhosa are a Bantu-speaking people of what is now the Eastern Cape of South Africa. The map shows their kingdom from 1783 to 1815, on the frontier of the Cape Colony.

They were cattle-keeping farmers, organised in chiefdoms that recognised a paramount king of the royal Tshawe line. Their language, isiXhosa, took its click sounds from long contact with Khoisan neighbours.

From 1779 the Xhosa fought nine frontier wars against Dutch settlers and then the British, the longest resistance to colonial rule in Africa, ending in 1879. In 1856 and 1857, after years of defeat, many Xhosa followed the prophecy of the girl Nongqawuse and killed their cattle, believing the dead would rise and the British would be swept away. The cattle-killing led to mass famine, and the colony took much of the remaining land.

The Xhosa later produced many leaders of the struggle against apartheid, among them Nelson Mandela.
